lawyer:
No one ----- For the Petitioner 
SS Halder with Probir Halder, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Asaduzzaman (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs
Md Salamatullah & others ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Md Hamidul Haque J: By these two Rules, opposite parties were directed to show cause as to why the proceedings of CR Case no. 555 of 1996 and CR Case No. 65 of 1996 pending in the Nalishi Adalat ‘Ka’ Anchal, Satkhira should not be quashed. 

 The petitioner in Criminal Misc. Case No. 767 of 1997 is accused in GR ease No. 555 of 1996.  Opposite party Md Salamatullah filed a petition of complaint before the Nalishi Adalat 'Ka' Anchal Satkhira alleging that the accused is a businessman and was known to him from before and he had been taking shrimp fries from complainant on different dates on credit. The accused took delivery of shrimp fries of law 30,01,303.00 during the year 1995, from the complainant and on demand the accused made payment of Taka 4.80,000.00 on different dates. Thereafter the accused came to the complainant on 2-7-95 at about 10-00 AM and handed over a cheque of Taka 26,11,303.00 in favour of the complainant which wits deposited by the complainant in bank on 25-7-95, and 23-8-95 for encashment but the cheque was dishonoured. Then the complainant issued a legal notice upon the dated on 29-6-96: The complainant met the dated on 30-7-1996 at about 3.00 PM at Dakhin Para Bus stand and there, in presence of witnesses, the accused refused to make the payment.' The complainant supplied shrimp fries on good faith on the representation of the accused that he would make payment. The learned Magistrate took cognizance against the accused under sections 406/420 of the Penal Code and issued warrant against accused. Thereafter the accused preferred the above Misc Case under section 561A of The CrPC for quashing the proceedings on the ground tilt no offence was committed under sections 406/420 of the Penal Code and the liability, if any, is a civil liability. 

 4. The petitioner of Criminal Misc Case No. 145 of 1997 is the accused in the other CR case 65 of 1996 which was also filed by the same complainant and Allegation made in the petition of complaint is also similar. In that case it was alleged the accused took delivery of shrimp fries of Taka 14,47,561.00 and made payment of taka 7,44,643.00 and refused to pay the balance amount. The petitioner of Misc. Case No 767 of 1997. 

 5. None appeared on behalf of the petitioners. Mr SS Halder with Mr Probir Halder, appeared on behalf of the complainant/opposite party and made detail submissions. Md Probir Halder at first has submitted that the accused petitioners in both the cases took delivery of shrimp fries from the complainant on the representation that the entire payment would be made and both the accused in recognition of the amount due to them, issued cheques for the balance amount in favour of the complainant but the cheques were dishonoured. According to him, this conduct of the accused petitioners shows that they had no intention to make the payment and they, by false inducement, got delivery of the shrimp fries having no intention to make full payment. He has further submitted that part payment was an eye-wash to deceive the complainant. Lastly, according to him though there cannot be an offence of cheating unless there is initial deception, the question whether there was any initial deception can be gathered only from the surrounding facts and circumstances and in support of his views, he referred to the case of Akamuddin vs State reported in 27 DLR (AD) 175. He has also referred to the case of Arifur Rahman alias Bablu vs Shontosh Kumar Sadhu reported in 46 DLR (AD) 180 to show that even if goods are taken on credit and the payment is not made, it will amount to an offence of cheating if there is specific promise of repayment. On the same point he also referred to the case of Mohadeu Proshad vs State of West Bengal reported in 1954 CrLJ (SC) page 1806. 

 6. On perusal of the petition of complaint of both the cases, we have found that the allegation against the accused petitioner is the same. It is clearly stated that the accused persons are known businessmen of the locality and they used to purchase shrimp fries from the complainant from before and in the year 1995 accused Asaduzzaman took delivery of shrimp fries on different dates and after making payment of Taka 4,80,000.00 further amount of Taka 30,91,303.00 remained unpaid and as against the accused Abdur Razzak the claim is that he made payment of Taka 7,44,643.00 and Taka 7,02,918.00 remained unpaid. So we have found that from the petition of complaint it is clear that the accused persons are businessmen, of the locality and they were known to the complainant from before and previously there was business transactions amongst them. It is also clear from the petition of complaint that the shrimp fries were purchased on different dates and after the end of the year specific amount was found due to the accused persons after deducting the payment made during that year on different dates. These are all ingredients of normal and regular business transaction. 

 9. Dishonouring of the cheque itself cannot he considered as an ingredient of the offence of cheating. Issuing of cheque implies that the persons issuing it had an account in the bank and that the amount of the cheque may be withdrawn from that hank account by the payee. But when such a cheque is dishonoured it will not be a criminal offence unless there is evidence to Show that after issuing of the cheque the person issuing it has done Something more to defraud the payee. Even such a cheque is issued with the knowledge that he has not such amount in the bank it will not amount to cheatihg if he has intention to deposit the money before the cheque is presented for encashment. In any case, our view is that simple dishonouring of a cheque itself is not an ingredient of cheating. 

 10. It is an established principle that to constitute an offence of cheating as described in section 415 of the Penal Code there must  be a specific allegation that the accused has initial intention of deceiving the complainant. It is also true that such intention can be gathered from the facts and circumstances because such intention normally is concealed in the mind and is not expressed. If there is allegation's that goods were delivered on credit on specific promise of repayment within a specific date but the payment was not made within the specific time, it may be inferred initial intention of deception. This is clear from the principle laid down in the case reported in 46 DLR (AD) 180. In this reported case our Appellate Division considered several decisions on this point specifically the decision given in 30 DLR 327 wherein it was held that when a person promised to pay the price of goods and on his undertaking to pay for the goods the goods were delivered to him and if he fails to pay no ease, of cheating would lie against him. In the case cited in 46 DLR (AD) 180 the accused took delivery of jute worth Taka 83,059.00 on the assurance  that he would pay Taka 40,000.00 in cash at the time of delivery and the rest of Taka 43,059.00 within three days. Considering this specific Condition and promise the  Appellate, Division held that in this particular case the delivery was made on the inducement of the accused and on his promise that payment of the rest amount would he paid within three days and so the court also held that there was ingredients of the offence of cheating. 

 11. In the light of the above principle, we have considered the case before us and we have found that the date of delivery of the shrimp fries, promised date of making payment etc are to be mentioned. The complainant mentioned about the entire transaction that took place in a whole year and only mentioned about the first date of demand and the date of refusal. In this particular case before us there is no allegation of any inducement or asp specific promise. It is clear to us that the transaction of the accused with the complainant was of the nature of regular and routine business transaction. In such a transaction, naturally there is no inducement and there is no specific promise. One party supplies goods on credit to the other party and the other party supplies goods on credit to the other party who makes payment. Under such transaction, after taking accounts at the end of the year some amount may fall due and this has exactly happened in the present case before us. 

 12. The facts of the case of Syed Ali Mir vs Syed Omar Ali as reported in 1990 BLD (AD) 168 (also in 42 DLR.(AD) 240) are similar to the facts of the present case. In that case also the accused purchased into from the complainant on credit and made some payment. Cheques issued were also dishonoured. The amount fell due after accounts at the end of the year. Under such circumstances, the court held that the liability was civil liability and the criminal courts should not be used as a contrivance to put pressure for repayment of dues. This principle is fully applicable in the present case before us. 

 13. The learned Advocate for the opposite party complainant has submitted that though the dates are not specifically mentioned in the petition of complaint, at the time of trial, the complainant may make specific allegation by mentioning the dates on which the transactions took place and the dates within which the accused persons promised to make the payment and as such he had argued that there should be trial first and the trial Court should decide whether there was any specific promise and whether there was initial deception. We cannot accept this view. When no such dates were Mentioned in the petition of complaint there is no scope of improving the case of a party by introducing such facts at the time of trial. 

 14. Mr SS Halder has also argued that in the absence of any specific agreement the proceedings cannot he quashed on the ground that liability is a civil liability. We also cannot appreciate this argument. All normal business transaction implies the existence of either an oral or written agreement. Even if a party makes purchase on credit normally some conditions are settled in between the purchaser and seller and this amounts to an agreement. It is not necessary that there should be a written agreement. In the instant case before us this the case of the complainant that he had business transaction, with the accused persons from befog and Nye have also found from our discussion above that the transaction in question was normal and routine transaction and as such the liability of the accused persons, if any, is civil liability. 

 In the result, both the Rules are made absolute. The proceedings of CR Case No. 555 of 1996 and CR Case No.65 of 1996 are quashed.
